title: Nasdaq 100 sinks 6% as chipmaker selloff deepens
article:
(Nov 6): A post-election slide in chipmakers snowballed, dragging the Nasdaq 100 down 6%, as investors bailed from the sector on speculation the Democratic sweep in Congress will usher in a new era of regulation for the artificial-intelligence (AI) industry.

The 11% plunge in a gauge of chip giants put the group on track for its worst week since the April 2025 tariff meltdown. Nvidia Corp slid 8%. Qualcomm Inc and Arm Holdings plc’s sank on underwhelming outlooks. Apple Inc plans to raise about US$7 billion from an investment-grade bond sale, adding to a flurry of tech issuance. Tesla Inc and SpaceX each lost 11%. Bitcoin fell 5.5%.

“The rotation out of chipmakers reflects growing concern about the pace and funding of AI spending due to the risk of more regulations after the blue wave, even as earnings remain resilient and valuations have reset sharply,” said Chris Murphy at Susquehanna International Group.

In a rush for safety, defensive industries like consumer staples and healthcare climbed. The swoon in tech shares also lifted bonds despite a rebound in oil prices. Haven currencies including the yen and the Swiss franc outperformed.

The AI trade is here to stay, but it remains volatile, and investors should not overlook some of the more boring areas of the market, according to Bob Edwards at Edwards Asset Management.

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 5% as chipmaker sell-off deepens

“We are not concerned about what the blue wave means for the buildout of AI, since the president still has the veto pen and data centres bring jobs and tax revenue,” he said.

Data centres have become an easy political target amid rising electricity bills. Bipartisan energy permitting reform could help by accelerating new power generation and transmission, while politicians will aim to ensure developers pay for the incremental grid infrastructure required to serve them, according to Jordan Jackson and Stephanie Aliaga at JPMorgan Asset Management.

The elections reinforced growing opposition to data centers, particularly in Texas and Ohio, where incoming Democratic governors favour tougher development conditions, they said. However, despite the backlash, statewide moratoriums have struggled to become law, accorrding to the strategists

“Politicians may now feel emboldened to adopt a harder stance but face competing pressures to protect ratepayers while attracting jobs, investment and tax revenues. AI remains an evolving public issue and is not yet a clear voter priority,” they noted.
• Microsoft Corp, one of Nscale’s primary customers, opted not to extend a contract at a Texas data centre with the startup ahead of its planned public offering, according to a person familiar with the matter.
• Micron Technology Inc has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a protracted labour dispute, according to people familiar with the matter, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial AI components.
• Amazon.com Inc is adding Uber Technologies Inc restaurant delivery perks on its shopping site for Prime members, forging a deeper partnership just a week after rival service DoorDash Inc agreed to acquire Instacart.
• Peloton Interactive Inc forecast holiday-quarter revenue that was slightly above Wall Street’s expectations, even as the fitness company projected a year-over-year sales decline and narrower profit margins.
• Wendy’s Co board unanimously rejected an offer from a group led by Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management to buy out the burger chain for about US$1.4 billion, saying the proposal substantially undervalues the company’s prospects and long-term earnings potential.

Some of the main moves in markets:
• The S&P 500 fell 3.7% as of 10.52am New York time
